newsitem.title: USA: CFTC's Born urges more overseas futures regulation.
newsitem.headline: CFTC's Born urges more overseas futures regulation.

text.p: The best way to level the international regulatory playing field in the futures industry would be to increase regulation abroad, rather than reduce domestic regulation, said Brooksley Born, chairman of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

In prepared remarks to the Futures Industry Association annual conference here, Born said the CFTC was addressing the competitive concerns of U.S. futures exchanges by working closely with foreign regulators to encourage more vigorous regulation of their markets.
"The playing field may be leveled more appropriately by raising the general level of regulation abroad than by reducing protections at home," Born said.
"I plan to continue the commission's strong commitment to its enforcement program," she said.

Born said that while the CFTC should be sensitive to the competitive needs of domestic markets, the exchanges must realize that the need for innovation does not diminish the CFTC's responsibility to protect customers against fraud, abuse, market manipulation and financial disruption.

"The commission must not allow preconceived regulatory notions to interfere with market innovation...(but) while we can and should be open-minded and flexible, we have a statutory obligation to enforce the law," Born said.

Born noted the CFTC has undertaken several initiatives to answer the competitive concerns of U.S. futures exchanges and work with overseas regulators to help them adopt regulatory systems comparable to those in the United States.

For example, at the end of November the CFTC will co-sponsor an international conference of regulators on physical delivery markets that will involve Britain's Securities and Investments Board and Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry.
She said that conference will focus on the special problems posed by physical delivery markets in international commodities, including market surveillance.
Born also noted complaints from domestic exchanges about competition from over-the-counter derivative markets, which the exchanges say are less regulated than they are.
But Born said that unlike U.S. futures exchanges, domestic OTC markets offer products that are used by sophisticated individuals and institutions rather than the general public.
"In my view, it is appropriate that regulation of this (OTC) market should be limited to issues relating to fraud and manipulation."
